title: React Programming Mastery
subtitle: Complete Guide from Beginner to Advanced
author: Systems Programming Experts

chapters.title: Introduction to JavaScript
chapters.description: Understanding JavaScript fundamentals and its role in modern web development

pages.title: What is JavaScript?
pages.content:
JavaScript is a high-level programming language used to create dynamic and interactive web applications. It runs directly in web browsers and allows developers to manipulate HTML content, handle events, and communicate with servers. JavaScript is one of the core technologies of the web alongside HTML and CSS.

Modern JavaScript is also used outside the browser with environments like Node.js, enabling developers to build full-stack applications using the same language.
pages.exampleCode: console.log('Hello JavaScript');

quiz.question: JavaScript is mainly used for:
quiz.explanation: JavaScript is used to create dynamic and interactive web pages.

pages.title: History of JavaScript
pages.content:
JavaScript was created in 1995 by Brendan Eich while working at Netscape. It was originally developed in just 10 days and was first called Mocha, then renamed LiveScript, and finally JavaScript.

JavaScript quickly became the standard language for web development. Today it is maintained by ECMA International under the ECMAScript specification.
pages.exampleCode:
// Example JavaScript code
console.log('JavaScript was created in 1995');
keyPoints: Now one of the most popular programming languages

quiz.question: Who created JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 1995.

pages.title: Why JavaScript is Important
pages.content:
JavaScript is essential for modern web development. It enables developers to create interactive websites, build full-stack applications, and develop mobile and desktop apps.

With frameworks such as React, Angular, and Vue, JavaScript powers most modern front-end applications.
pages.exampleCode:
let message = 'JavaScript powers modern web apps';
console.log(message);
keyPoints: Also used in backend with Node.js

quiz.question: Which framework is built using JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: React is a JavaScript framework/library.

pages.title: Where JavaScript Runs
pages.content:
JavaScript can run in multiple environments. Traditionally, it runs inside web browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. However, with Node.js, JavaScript can also run on servers.

This allows developers to build both frontend and backend applications using the same language.
pages.exampleCode:
// JavaScript can run in browsers
console.log('Running in browser console');
keyPoints: Can be used for mobile and desktop apps

quiz.question: Which environment allows JavaScript to run on the server?
quiz.explanation: Node.js allows JavaScript to run on the server.

pages.title: Adding JavaScript to HTML
pages.content:
JavaScript can be added to HTML in three ways: inline, internal, and external.

Inline JavaScript is written directly inside HTML elements. Internal JavaScript is written inside the script tag in an HTML file. External JavaScript is written in a separate .js file and linked to HTML.
pages.exampleCode:
<script>
console.log('JavaScript inside HTML');
</script>

quiz.question: Which tag is used to include JavaScript in HTML?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript is added using the script tag.

pages.title: Your First JavaScript Program
pages.content: The most common way to display output in JavaScript during development is using console.log(). The console displays messages that help developers debug and understand program behavior.
pages.exampleCode: console.log('My first JavaScript program');

quiz.question: Which function prints output in the console?
quiz.explanation: console.log() prints messages in the browser console.

chapters.title: Variables
chapters.description: Understanding variables and how to store data in JavaScript

pages.title: What is a Variable?
pages.content:
A variable is a container used to store data values in a program. In JavaScript, variables allow developers to store numbers, strings, objects, arrays, and other data types.

Variables are declared using keywords such as var, let, or const.
pages.exampleCode:
let name = 'John';
console.log(name);
keyPoints: Used to hold different types of values
Declared using var, let, or const

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a variable?
quiz.explanation: Variables are used to store data.

pages.title: Using var
pages.content:
The var keyword was used in older JavaScript versions to declare variables. Variables declared with var are function-scoped and can be redeclared within the same scope.

However, var is not commonly used in modern JavaScript because it can cause unexpected behavior.
pages.exampleCode:
var age = 25;
console.log(age);

quiz.question: Which keyword was used in older JavaScript to declare variables?
quiz.explanation: var was used in older JavaScript versions.

pages.title: Using let
pages.content: The let keyword was introduced in ES6. It allows developers to declare variables with block scope. Unlike var, variables declared with let cannot be redeclared in the same scope.
pages.exampleCode:
let score = 100;
console.log(score);

quiz.question: Which keyword provides block scope?
quiz.explanation: let creates block-scoped variables.

pages.title: Using const
pages.content:
The const keyword is used to declare variables whose values should not change. Once a value is assigned to a const variable, it cannot be reassigned.

Const variables must be initialized when declared.
pages.exampleCode:
const pi = 3.14;
console.log(pi);

quiz.question: Which keyword is used for constant values?
quiz.explanation: const declares variables that cannot be reassigned.

pages.title: Variable Scope
pages.content:
Scope determines where variables can be accessed. JavaScript has two main scopes: global scope and block scope.

Global variables can be accessed anywhere in the program, while block-scoped variables exist only inside the block where they are declared.
keyPoints: Block scope variables limited to blocks
let and const support block scope

quiz.question: Which keyword supports block scope?
quiz.explanation: let supports block scope.

pages.title: Variable Naming Rules
pages.content:
JavaScript variables must follow certain naming rules. Variable names should start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign. They cannot start with numbers and should not use reserved keywords.

Good variable names improve code readability and maintainability.
pages.exampleCode:
let userName = 'Alice';
let totalPrice = 100;
keyPoints: Variable names cannot start with numbers

quiz.question: Which variable name is valid?
quiz.explanation: userName follows JavaScript naming rules.

chapters.title: Data Types
chapters.description: Understanding primitive and non-primitive data types in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Data Types?
pages.content:
Data types define the type of value stored in a variable. JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, meaning variables do not need an explicit type declaration. The data type is automatically determined based on the value assigned.

JavaScript data types are divided into two main categories: Primitive and Non-Primitive (Reference) types.
keyPoints: Defines the type of value stored

quiz.question: JavaScript is a:
quiz.explanation: JavaScript automatically determines variable types.

pages.title: String Data Type
pages.content:
A string represents textual data in JavaScript. Strings can be written using single quotes, double quotes, or backticks.

Strings are commonly used for storing names, messages, and text content.
keyPoints: Can use single, double, or backtick quotes

quiz.question: Which symbol allows template literals?
quiz.explanation: Backticks (`) allow template literals.

pages.title: Number Data Type
pages.content: The number data type represents numeric values such as integers and floating-point numbers. JavaScript uses a single number type for all numeric values.

quiz.question: Which data type represents numbers?
quiz.explanation: Number represents numeric values.

pages.title: Boolean Data Type
pages.content: A boolean data type represents logical values. It has only two possible values: true and false. Booleans are commonly used in conditional statements and comparisons.

quiz.question: How many values does Boolean have?
quiz.explanation: Boolean has two values: true and false.

pages.title: Null and Undefined
pages.content: Null represents an intentional absence of value. Undefined means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value.

quiz.question: What does undefined mean?
quiz.explanation: Undefined means the variable has no assigned value.

pages.title: Symbol and BigInt
pages.content: Symbol is a unique and immutable primitive data type used mainly for object property keys. BigInt is used to represent very large integers beyond the limit of the Number type.

quiz.question: Which type stores very large numbers?
quiz.explanation: BigInt stores integers larger than Number can handle.

pages.title: Checking Data Types
pages.content: JavaScript provides the typeof operator to determine the type of a variable. It helps developers debug and understand the data they are working with.
keyPoints: Returns the data type as a string

quiz.question: Which operator checks data type?
quiz.explanation: typeof returns the type of a variable.

chapters.title: Operators
chapters.description: Understanding different types of operators used in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Operators?
pages.content:
Operators are symbols used to perform operations on variables and values. They allow JavaScript programs to perform tasks such as calculations, comparisons, and logical evaluations.

Operators play an essential role in building expressions and controlling program logic.

quiz.question: Operators are used to:
quiz.explanation: Operators perform operations on variables and values.

pages.title: Arithmetic Operators
pages.content: Arithmetic operators are used to perform mathematical operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
pages.exampleCode:
let a = 10;
let b = 5;

console.log(a + b); // Addition
console.log(a - b); // Subtraction
console.log(a * b); // Multiplication
console.log(a / b); // Division
console.log(a % b); // Modulus

quiz.question: Which operator gives the remainder?
quiz.explanation: The modulus operator (%) returns the remainder.

pages.title: Assignment Operators
pages.content: Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables. The most common assignment operator is =, but JavaScript also provides compound assignment operators.

quiz.question: Which operator assigns a value?
quiz.explanation: The = operator assigns values.

pages.title: Comparison Operators
pages.content: Comparison operators are used to compare two values and return a boolean result (true or false). They are commonly used in conditions and loops.

quiz.question: Which operator checks strict equality?
quiz.explanation: === checks value and type equality.

pages.title: Logical Operators
pages.content: Logical operators are used to combine multiple conditions. They return boolean values based on logical relationships.

quiz.question: Which operator means logical AND?
quiz.explanation: && represents logical AND.

pages.title: Increment and Decrement
pages.content: Increment (++) increases a variable by one, while decrement (--) decreases a variable by one. These operators are commonly used in loops.

quiz.question: Which operator increases value by one?
quiz.explanation: ++ increases value by one.

pages.title: Operator Precedence
pages.content: Operator precedence determines the order in which operations are executed in an expression. Multiplication and division have higher precedence than addition and subtraction.
pages.exampleCode:
let result = 10 + 5 * 2;
console.log(result);

quiz.question: Which operation runs first?
quiz.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence.

chapters.title: Control Statements
chapters.description: Understanding conditional statements used to control program flow

pages.title: What are Control Statements?
pages.content:
Control statements determine the order in which code is executed in a program. They allow developers to execute different blocks of code depending on conditions.

In JavaScript, conditional statements are commonly used to perform decision-making operations.

quiz.question: Control statements are used for:
quiz.explanation: Control statements allow programs to make decisions.

pages.title: if Statement
pages.content: The if statement executes a block of code only if a specified condition evaluates to true. It is the simplest form of conditional statement.
keyPoints: Executes code if condition is true

quiz.question: Which statement runs code when condition is true?
quiz.explanation: The if statement runs code when a condition is true.

pages.title: if...else Statement
pages.content: The if...else statement executes one block of code if the condition is true and another block if the condition is false.

quiz.question: What happens if an if condition is false?
quiz.explanation: The else block runs when the condition is false.

pages.title: else if Ladder
pages.content: The else if ladder allows checking multiple conditions sequentially. The first condition that evaluates to true executes its block.

quiz.question: Which statement checks multiple conditions?
quiz.explanation: The else if ladder allows multiple condition checks.

pages.title: Switch Statement
pages.content: The switch statement evaluates an expression and executes the matching case block. It is useful when there are many possible values to check.
keyPoints: Default runs if no case matches

quiz.question: Which keyword exits a switch case?
quiz.explanation: break stops execution of the switch block.

pages.title: Nested Conditions
pages.content: Nested conditions occur when one conditional statement is placed inside another. This is useful when multiple dependent conditions need to be checked.

quiz.question: What is a nested condition?
quiz.explanation: Nested conditions place one condition inside another.

chapters.title: Loops
chapters.description: Understanding loops used to execute repeated operations in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Loops?
pages.content: Loops allow developers to execute a block of code multiple times without rewriting the same code. They are useful when performing repetitive tasks such as printing numbers, iterating through arrays, or processing large datasets.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of loops?
quiz.explanation: Loops repeat a block of code multiple times.

pages.title: for Loop
pages.content: The for loop is the most commonly used loop in JavaScript. It runs a block of code a specific number of times and contains three parts: initialization, condition, and increment/decrement.

quiz.question: Which loop is best when the number of iterations is known?
quiz.explanation: The for loop is ideal when the iteration count is known.

pages.title: while Loop
pages.content: The while loop executes code as long as a specified condition remains true. It checks the condition before executing the loop body.
keyPoints: Useful when iteration count is unknown

quiz.question: Which loop checks the condition before executing?
quiz.explanation: The while loop checks the condition before execution.

pages.title: do...while Loop
pages.content: The do...while loop executes the code block at least once before checking the condition. The condition is evaluated after the loop body runs.
keyPoints: Useful when code must run initially

quiz.question: Which loop runs at least once?
quiz.explanation: The do...while loop executes the code block before checking the condition.

pages.title: Break Statement
pages.content: The break statement is used to terminate a loop immediately. When break is encountered, the loop stops executing and control moves to the next statement after the loop.
keyPoints: Common in loops and switch statements

quiz.question: What does break do in a loop?
quiz.explanation: The break statement stops loop execution.

pages.title: Continue Statement
pages.content: The continue statement skips the current iteration of a loop and moves to the next iteration. It does not terminate the loop entirely.

quiz.question: What does continue do?
quiz.explanation: continue skips the current loop iteration.

pages.title: Nested Loops
pages.content: Nested loops occur when one loop is placed inside another. They are commonly used for working with multi-dimensional data such as matrices or tables.
keyPoints: Inner loop runs fully for each outer iteration

quiz.question: What is a nested loop?
quiz.explanation: Nested loops are loops placed inside other loops.

chapters.title: Functions
chapters.description: Understanding functions and how they help create reusable code in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Functions?
pages.content:
A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task. Functions allow developers to avoid repeating the same code multiple times.

Functions are executed when they are called or invoked.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a function?
quiz.explanation: Functions help reuse code.

pages.title: Function Declaration
pages.content: A function declaration defines a named function using the function keyword. These functions can be called anywhere in the code due to hoisting.

quiz.question: Which keyword defines a function?
quiz.explanation: Functions are declared using the function keyword.

pages.title: Function Expressions
pages.content: A function expression assigns a function to a variable. Unlike function declarations, function expressions are not hoisted.

quiz.question: Where is a function stored in a function expression?
quiz.explanation: Function expressions store functions in variables.

pages.title: Arrow Functions
pages.content: Arrow functions were introduced in ES6 to provide a shorter syntax for writing functions. They are commonly used in modern JavaScript applications.

quiz.question: Which symbol is used in arrow functions?
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions use the => syntax.

pages.title: Parameters and Arguments
pages.content: Parameters are variables listed in the function definition. Arguments are the actual values passed to the function when it is called.

quiz.question: Values passed to functions are called:
quiz.explanation: Arguments are values passed to functions.

pages.title: Return Values
pages.content: Functions can return values using the return statement. This allows the result of a function to be used elsewhere in the program.

quiz.question: Which keyword returns a value from a function?
quiz.explanation: return sends a value back from a function.

pages.title: Default Parameters
pages.content: Default parameters allow functions to assign default values if no argument is provided. This prevents errors and simplifies function usage.

quiz.question: Default parameters were introduced in:
quiz.explanation: Default parameters were introduced in ES6.

chapters.title: Arrays
chapters.description: Understanding arrays and how to store multiple values in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Arrays?
pages.content:
An array is a data structure used to store multiple values in a single variable. Instead of creating separate variables for each value, arrays allow developers to store and manage collections of data efficiently.

Each value in an array is called an element and is accessed using an index. The index of an array starts from 0.
pages.exampleCode:
let fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange'];
console.log(fruits);

quiz.question: What is the index of the first element in an array?
quiz.explanation: Array indexes start from 0.

pages.title: Creating Arrays
pages.content: Arrays can be created using square brackets or the Array constructor. The most common method is using square brackets.

quiz.question: Which symbol is used to create arrays?
quiz.explanation: Arrays are created using square brackets [].

pages.title: Accessing Array Elements
pages.content: Array elements are accessed using their index. Since arrays start at index 0, the first element is accessed using index 0.

quiz.question: How do you access the second element in an array?
quiz.explanation: Index 1 represents the second element.

pages.title: Adding and Removing Elements
pages.content:
JavaScript provides several built-in methods to add or remove elements from arrays.

push() adds an element to the end of an array.
pop() removes the last element.
unshift() adds an element to the beginning.
shift() removes the first element.

quiz.question: Which method adds an element at the end of an array?
quiz.explanation: push() adds elements to the end of an array.

pages.title: Array Length
pages.content: The length property returns the number of elements in an array. It is useful when iterating through arrays.
pages.exampleCode:
let fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange'];

console.log(fruits.length);

quiz.question: Which property returns the number of elements in an array?
quiz.explanation: length returns the total elements in an array.

pages.title: Iterating Arrays
pages.content: Arrays can be iterated using loops such as for loop or forEach method. Iteration allows developers to access each element of an array.

quiz.question: Which method iterates through array elements?
quiz.explanation: forEach iterates through array elements.

chapters.title: Objects
chapters.description: Understanding objects and how to store structured data in JavaScript

pages.title: What are Objects?
pages.content:
Objects are collections of key-value pairs used to represent structured data. Each key is called a property, and the value can be any data type including numbers, strings, arrays, or even functions.

Objects are commonly used to represent real-world entities such as users, products, or courses.
keyPoints: Values can be any data type

quiz.question: What does an object store?
quiz.explanation: Objects store data as key-value pairs.

pages.title: Creating Objects
pages.content: Objects can be created using object literals with curly braces {}. This is the most common way to create objects in JavaScript.

quiz.question: Which symbol is used to create objects?
quiz.explanation: Objects are created using curly braces {}.

pages.title: Accessing Object Properties
pages.content: Object properties can be accessed using dot notation or bracket notation. Dot notation is commonly used when property names are known.

quiz.question: Which syntax accesses object properties?
quiz.explanation: Both dot and bracket notation access properties.

pages.title: Adding and Removing Properties
pages.content: JavaScript allows developers to add new properties or remove existing ones from objects dynamically.

quiz.question: Which keyword removes an object property?
quiz.explanation: delete removes object properties.

pages.title: Object Methods
pages.content: Objects can contain functions called methods. Methods define behaviors associated with the object.

quiz.question: Functions inside objects are called:
quiz.explanation: Functions inside objects are called methods.

pages.title: The 'this' Keyword
pages.content: The 'this' keyword refers to the current object. It allows object methods to access properties within the same object.

quiz.question: What does 'this' refer to in an object method?
quiz.explanation: this refers to the current object.

chapters.title: DOM Manipulation
chapters.description: Understanding how JavaScript interacts with HTML using the Document Object Model

pages.title: What is the DOM?
pages.content: The DOM (Document Object Model) represents the structure of an HTML document as a tree of objects. Each element in an HTML page becomes a node in the DOM tree. JavaScript can use the DOM to access, modify, and manipulate HTML elements dynamically.
pages.exampleCode: console.log(document);
keyPoints: JavaScript can interact with HTML using DOM
DOM is structured like a tree

quiz.question: What does DOM stand for?
quiz.explanation: DOM stands for Document Object Model.

pages.title: Selecting HTML Elements
pages.content: JavaScript provides several methods to select HTML elements from the DOM. These include getElementById, getElementsByClassName, getElementsByTagName, and querySelector.
keyPoints: DOM selection is used before manipulation

quiz.question: Which method selects an element by ID?
quiz.explanation: getElementById selects elements by their ID.

pages.title: Changing Element Content
pages.content: JavaScript allows developers to modify the content of HTML elements using properties like innerText, innerHTML, and textContent.
pages.exampleCode:
let heading = document.getElementById('title');
heading.innerText = 'Welcome to JavaScript';

quiz.question: Which property changes text content of an element?
quiz.explanation: innerText changes the text inside an element.

pages.title: Changing Styles
pages.content: JavaScript can change the CSS styles of HTML elements using the style property. This allows dynamic updates to page appearance.

quiz.question: Which property modifies CSS styles in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: style is used to modify CSS properties.

pages.title: Creating Elements
pages.content: JavaScript can dynamically create new HTML elements using document.createElement(). These elements can then be added to the DOM using appendChild() or append().

quiz.question: Which method creates a new HTML element?
quiz.explanation: createElement creates new HTML elements.

pages.title: Removing Elements
pages.content: Elements can be removed from the DOM using remove() or removeChild(). This helps dynamically update page content.
pages.exampleCode:
let element = document.getElementById('item');
element.remove();

quiz.question: Which method removes an element from the DOM?
quiz.explanation: remove() deletes an element from the DOM.

chapters.title: Events
chapters.description: Understanding how JavaScript responds to user interactions using events

pages.title: What are Events?
pages.content:
Events are actions or occurrences that happen in the browser, usually triggered by the user. Examples include clicking a button, typing on a keyboard, or submitting a form.

JavaScript can listen for these events and execute specific code when they occur.
keyPoints: Examples include click, input, and submit

quiz.question: What triggers an event in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Events are triggered by user interactions like clicks or typing.

pages.title: Event Listeners
pages.content: Event listeners allow JavaScript to detect when a specific event occurs on an element. The addEventListener() method is commonly used to attach events.
keyPoints: Can listen to many event types

quiz.question: Which method attaches an event listener?
quiz.explanation: addEventListener is used to attach events.

pages.title: Click Events
pages.content: Click events occur when a user clicks an HTML element such as a button, link, or image. They are commonly used to trigger actions like opening menus or submitting data.

quiz.question: Which event occurs when a user clicks a button?
quiz.explanation: The click event triggers when a button is clicked.

pages.title: Form Events
pages.content: Form events occur when users interact with forms. Examples include submit, input, change, and focus events.
keyPoints: submit triggers when form is submitted

quiz.question: Which method prevents form refresh?
quiz.explanation: preventDefault prevents default browser behavior.

pages.title: Keyboard Events
pages.content: Keyboard events occur when users press keys on the keyboard. Common keyboard events include keydown, keyup, and keypress.

quiz.question: Which event occurs when a key is pressed?
quiz.explanation: Both keypress and keydown can detect key presses.

pages.title: Event Bubbling
pages.content: Event bubbling occurs when an event starts from the target element and propagates upward through its parent elements. This allows parent elements to respond to events triggered on child elements.
keyPoints: Event moves from child to parent

quiz.question: Event bubbling moves from:
quiz.explanation: Event bubbling moves from the child element to its parent.

chapters.title: ES6 Features
chapters.description: Understanding modern JavaScript features introduced in ES6

pages.title: Introduction to ES6
pages.content:
ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) is a major update to JavaScript that introduced many modern features. These features simplify JavaScript development and improve readability and maintainability.

Modern frameworks like React and Node.js heavily rely on ES6 syntax.
pages.exampleCode:
let message = 'Welcome to ES6';
console.log(message);

quiz.question: What does ES6 stand for?
quiz.explanation: ES6 stands for ECMAScript 6.

pages.title: let and const
pages.content:
ES6 introduced let and const to replace var. These provide block scope and improve variable management.

let allows reassignment, while const creates constant variables.

quiz.question: Which keyword creates a constant variable?
quiz.explanation: const creates variables that cannot be reassigned.

pages.title: Arrow Functions
pages.content: Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax for writing functions. They are widely used in modern JavaScript and React development.
pages.exampleCode:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;

console.log(add(5, 3));

quiz.question: Which syntax defines an arrow function?
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions use the => syntax.

pages.title: Template Literals
pages.content: Template literals allow embedding variables inside strings using backticks (`). They make string concatenation easier and cleaner.

quiz.question: Which symbol is used for template literals?
quiz.explanation: Template literals use backticks (`).

pages.title: Destructuring
pages.content: Destructuring allows developers to extract values from arrays or objects into separate variables. It simplifies code when working with complex data structures.

quiz.question: Destructuring is used to:
quiz.explanation: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or objects.

pages.title: Spread Operator
pages.content: The spread operator (...) allows expanding elements of arrays or objects. It is commonly used for copying arrays and merging objects.

quiz.question: Which symbol represents the spread operator?
quiz.explanation: The spread operator uses three dots (...).

pages.title: Modules
pages.content: ES6 introduced modules that allow JavaScript files to export and import functionality. This helps organize code into reusable components.

quiz.question: Which keyword imports modules?
quiz.explanation: import is used to load modules.

chapters.title: Promises
chapters.description: Understanding asynchronous programming using JavaScript Promises

pages.title: What are Promises?
pages.content: A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. Promises allow JavaScript to handle tasks that take time to complete, such as fetching data from a server.

quiz.question: Promises are mainly used for:
quiz.explanation: Promises handle asynchronous operations like API requests.

pages.title: Promise States
pages.content:
A Promise has three possible states: Pending, Fulfilled, and Rejected.

Pending means the operation is still running. Fulfilled means the operation completed successfully. Rejected means the operation failed.

quiz.question: How many states does a Promise have?
quiz.explanation: Promises have three states: Pending, Fulfilled, and Rejected.

pages.title: Creating Promises
pages.content: Promises are created using the Promise constructor. It takes a function with two parameters: resolve and reject.

quiz.question: Which keyword creates a Promise?
quiz.explanation: Promises are created using the Promise constructor.

pages.title: Using .then()
pages.content: The .then() method is used to handle successful completion of a Promise. It receives the resolved value as its argument.

quiz.question: Which method handles successful Promise results?
quiz.explanation: .then() handles successful promise results.

pages.title: Using .catch()
pages.content: The .catch() method handles errors in Promises. It executes when a Promise is rejected.

quiz.question: Which method handles Promise errors?
quiz.explanation: .catch() handles rejected promises.

pages.title: Promise Chaining
pages.content: Promise chaining allows multiple asynchronous operations to run sequentially using multiple .then() methods.
pages.exampleCode:
fetch('https://api.example.com/data')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.log(error));

quiz.question: Promise chaining is done using:
quiz.explanation: Promise chaining uses multiple .then() calls.

chapters.title: Async / Await
chapters.description: Understanding modern asynchronous programming using async and await

pages.title: Asynchronous Programming
pages.content:
Asynchronous programming allows JavaScript to perform tasks without blocking the execution of other code. This is useful for operations that take time such as API calls, file loading, and database requests.

Instead of waiting for a task to complete, JavaScript continues executing other code.
keyPoints: Used for API calls and timers

quiz.question: What does asynchronous programming allow?
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous programming allows tasks to run without blocking the main thread.

pages.title: Async Functions
pages.content: An async function is a function declared using the async keyword. It always returns a Promise. Inside an async function, developers can use the await keyword to handle asynchronous operations.

quiz.question: What does an async function return?
quiz.explanation: Async functions always return a Promise.

pages.title: Await Keyword
pages.content: The await keyword pauses execution of an async function until the Promise is resolved. It can only be used inside async functions.

quiz.question: Where can await be used?
quiz.explanation: await can only be used inside async functions.

pages.title: Error Handling with try...catch
pages.content: Errors in async/await code can be handled using try...catch blocks. This ensures the application can gracefully handle failures in asynchronous operations.

quiz.question: Which block handles errors?
quiz.explanation: catch handles errors in try...catch blocks.

pages.title: Converting Promises to Async/Await
pages.content: Async/await is built on top of Promises. Instead of chaining multiple .then() methods, developers can use await to write cleaner and more readable code.

quiz.question: Async/await is built on top of:
quiz.explanation: Async/await is based on Promises.

chapters.title: Fetch API & API Integration
chapters.description: Understanding how JavaScript communicates with servers using the Fetch API

pages.title: What is Fetch API?
pages.content:
The Fetch API is a modern JavaScript interface used to make HTTP requests to servers. It allows web applications to retrieve or send data asynchronously.

Fetch is commonly used to communicate with REST APIs and load data dynamically into web pages.

quiz.question: What does the Fetch API do?
quiz.explanation: Fetch API is used to send and receive data from servers.

pages.title: Making GET Requests
pages.content: GET requests are used to retrieve data from a server. Fetch makes GET requests by default when only the URL is provided.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method retrieves data?
quiz.explanation: GET requests retrieve data from the server.

pages.title: Making POST Requests
pages.content: POST requests send data to the server. This is commonly used when submitting forms or creating new records in a database.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method sends data to server?
quiz.explanation: POST sends data to the server.

pages.title: Handling JSON Data
pages.content: Most APIs return data in JSON format. The response.json() method converts the response into usable JavaScript objects.

quiz.question: Which method converts API response to JSON?
quiz.explanation: response.json() converts API data to JSON.

pages.title: Error Handling in Fetch
pages.content: Errors can occur during API requests due to network issues or server problems. JavaScript uses catch() or try/catch with async/await to handle these errors.
pages.exampleCode:
fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.log('Error:', error));

quiz.question: Which method handles fetch errors?
quiz.explanation: catch handles errors in fetch requests.

interviewQuestions.question: What is JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: JavaScript is a high-level programming language used to create dynamic and interactive web applications.

interviewQuestions.question: Is JavaScript a compiled or interpreted language?
interviewQuestions.answer: JavaScript is primarily an interpreted language executed by browsers using JavaScript engines.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the main data types in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null, Symbol, BigInt, and Object.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between let, var, and const?
interviewQuestions.answer: var has function scope, let and const have block scope. const cannot be reassigned.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a variable in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: A variable is a container used to store data values.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a function?
interviewQuestions.answer: A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an array?
interviewQuestions.answer: An array is a data structure used to store multiple values in a single variable.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an object in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: An object is a collection of key-value pairs used to represent structured data.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the DOM?
interviewQuestions.answer: The DOM (Document Object Model) represents HTML documents as objects that JavaScript can manipulate.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an event in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: An event is an action that occurs in the browser such as clicking a button or typing on a keyboard.

interviewQuestions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving variable and function declarations to the top of their scope during compilation.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
interviewQuestions.answer: == compares values after type conversion, while === compares both value and data type.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a callback function?
interviewQuestions.answer: A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a closure?
interviewQuestions.answer: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has finished executing.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
interviewQuestions.answer: null represents an intentional empty value, while undefined means a variable has been declared but not assigned.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the typeof operator?
interviewQuestions.answer: typeof is used to determine the data type of a variable.

interviewQuestions.question: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: Destructuring allows extracting values from arrays or objects into variables.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the spread operator?
interviewQuestions.answer: The spread operator (...) expands elements of arrays or objects.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between map() and forEach()?
interviewQuestions.answer: map() returns a new array, while forEach() executes a function for each element but does not return a new array.

interviewQuestions.question: What is event bubbling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Event bubbling is the process where events propagate from child elements to parent elements.

interviewQuestions.question: What are promises in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: Promises represent the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the states of a Promise?
interviewQuestions.answer: Pending, Fulfilled, and Rejected.

interviewQuestions.question: What is async/await?
interviewQuestions.answer: Async/await simplifies working with Promises and allows writing asynchronous code like synchronous code.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the Fetch API?
interviewQuestions.answer: Fetch API is used to make HTTP requests to servers.

interviewQuestions.question: What is JSON?
interviewQuestions.answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight format for storing and exchanging data.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous programming?
interviewQuestions.answer: Synchronous code runs sequentially, while asynchronous code allows tasks to run without blocking execution.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the event loop?
interviewQuestions.answer: The event loop handles asynchronous callbacks and ensures non-blocking execution in JavaScript.

interviewQuestions.question: What are arrow functions?
interviewQuestions.answer: Arrow functions are a shorter syntax for writing functions introduced in ES6.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between function declaration and function expression?
interviewQuestions.answer: Function declarations are hoisted, while function expressions are not.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the this keyword?
interviewQuestions.answer: The this keyword refers to the current object executing the function.

interviewQuestions.question: What are template literals?
interviewQuestions.answer: Template literals allow embedding variables in strings using backticks.

interviewQuestions.question: What is local storage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Local storage allows storing data in the browser with no expiration date.

interviewQuestions.question: What is session storage?
interviewQuestions.answer: Session storage stores data only for the duration of the browser session.

interviewQuestions.question: What is debouncing?
interviewQuestions.answer: Debouncing limits how often a function executes during repeated events.

interviewQuestions.question: What is throttling?
interviewQuestions.answer: Throttling ensures a function executes at most once within a specified time interval.

interviewQuestions.question: What are JavaScript modules?
interviewQuestions.answer: Modules allow splitting code into reusable files using export and import.

interviewQuestions.question: What is strict mode?
interviewQuestions.answer: Strict mode enforces stricter parsing and error handling in JavaScript.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
interviewQuestions.answer: They control the value of this in functions. call and apply invoke functions immediately, while bind returns a new function.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
interviewQuestions.answer: Shallow copy copies references, while deep copy duplicates nested objects.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a higher-order function?
interviewQuestions.answer: A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between let and const?
interviewQuestions.answer: let allows reassignment while const does not allow reassignment.

interviewQuestions.question: What does NaN mean?
interviewQuestions.answer: NaN stands for Not-a-Number and represents an invalid numeric value.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between slice() and splice()?
interviewQuestions.answer: slice returns a new array, while splice modifies the original array.

interviewQuestions.question: What does the Array.isArray() method do?
interviewQuestions.answer: It checks whether a value is an array.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a prototype in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer: A prototype is an object from which other objects inherit properties.

interviewQuestions.question: What is garbage collection?
interviewQuestions.answer: Garbage collection automatically removes unused memory from JavaScript programs.

interviewQuestions.question: What is optional chaining?
interviewQuestions.answer: Optional chaining (?.) safely accesses nested object properties without errors.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between window and document?
interviewQuestions.answer: window represents the browser window, while document represents the HTML document loaded in it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the debugger statement?
interviewQuestions.answer: The debugger statement pauses code execution for debugging.
